title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what is over, what was aimed at, what was expected

questions.prompt: Complete this line from the yearly report of an association in Kairouan. Only the sentence itself tells you which form to choose: "Last winter the volunteers printed every notice in three languages so that every family in the district ___ it."

options.text: can read
will read
would have read
could read

questions.explanation: "could read" is the form: a clause of purpose carries a modal, and that modal follows the tense of the main verb — can and will after a present, a present perfect or a future, could and would after a past. The main verb here is printed, and Last winter closes the question, so the past side is the only one open. "can read" is the present member of the pair, and it leaves the sentence with a past main verb and a present purpose, which no English sentence does. "will read" makes the same clash with the future. And "would have read" adds a perfect that says the reading was expected and did not happen; a purpose clause tells what was wanted at the time of the action, and it never reports afterwards whether it worked.

questions.prompt: An editor is shortening the lines of a school magazine before it goes to the printer. She has this one in front of her: "Rania takes the six o'clock bus so that she can be at the workshop before eight." She wants a shorter line that says exactly the same thing. Which line does she print?

options.text: Rania takes the six o'clock bus to be at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus for being at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus so to be at the workshop before eight.
Rania takes the six o'clock bus, so she is at the workshop before eight.

questions.explanation: "Rania takes the six o'clock bus to be at the workshop before eight." is the shorter line: the two halves of the original have the same subject, Rania takes and she can be, and when the person is the same the clause is not needed at all — an infinitive of purpose carries the aim on its own, and it attaches to the subject already there. "Rania takes the six o'clock bus for being at the workshop before eight." copies your own language, which puts a preposition and a verbal noun in front of an aim; English gives an aim with to and the base verb. "Rania takes the six o'clock bus so to be at the workshop before eight." keeps half of so that and drops the half that matters: so that must be followed by a subject and a verb, and so on its own is never followed by an infinitive. And "Rania takes the six o'clock bus, so she is at the workshop before eight." is correct English but has changed the message: it now reports what happens every morning instead of what she is aiming at, and the editor was told to keep the meaning.

questions.prompt: Khaled started work at a bakery in Bizerte in June, and the first weeks were hard: he had never in his life got out of bed before dawn. It is now September, and the four o'clock alarm costs him nothing at all. Which sentence does he say about himself today?

options.text: I used to get up at four.
I am used to get up at four.
I am used to getting up at four.
I am not used to getting up at four.

questions.explanation: "I am used to getting up at four." says what September has changed: be used to means that something has stopped feeling strange, it takes a noun or an -ing form after it, and it is true of him now. "I used to get up at four." is the other structure altogether, three fixed words plus a base verb, and it would announce that the four o'clock mornings are behind him — but he is still at the bakery. "I am used to get up at four." starts on the right structure and then puts a base verb where the -ing form belongs; after the to of be used to, English never uses an infinitive. And "I am not used to getting up at four." is built correctly and says the opposite of the situation: it is what he could have said in June, not what he says once the alarm costs him nothing.

questions.prompt: Two classmates say almost the same words to Sonia about the same chapter of history. One of them speaks to her on the evening before the test; the other speaks to her on the way out of the examination room. Which sentence belongs to the one who is speaking after the test?

options.text: You should revise the last chapter.
You should have revised the last chapter.
You shouldn't revise the last chapter.
You had better revise the last chapter tonight.

questions.explanation: "You should have revised the last chapter." belongs to the classmate who speaks afterwards: should have plus the past participle looks back at something that was not done and can no longer be done, and it turns advice into a reproach. "You should revise the last chapter." is advice with the door still open, so it can only be said while there is still an evening left. "You had better revise the last chapter tonight." is advice as well, more urgent than the first and dated by the word tonight, which no one says once the paper has been handed in. And "You shouldn't revise the last chapter." advises against doing something, which fits neither moment: nobody tells a classmate to leave a chapter out, and in any case a present modal cannot reach a test that is over.

questions.prompt: A dispatcher in Sfax is following one of his delivery vans. It left the depot at six this morning, the journey takes about seven hours, and the office clock now says half past three. He turns to his colleague and says: "It should have reached Tataouine by now." What is he doing with those words?

options.text: He is blaming the driver for leaving too late.
He is saying what he expects to be true at this moment.
He is regretting a decision he took this morning.
He is ordering the driver to telephone him before four o'clock.

questions.explanation: "He is saying what he expects to be true at this moment." is what the sentence does: should have has a second value beside regret, an assumption, and the dispatcher is simply counting — six o'clock plus seven hours, against a clock that says half past three. "He is blaming the driver for leaving too late." reads a reproach into a calculation; a reproach needs somebody who failed to do what was expected, and here everything has gone to plan. "He is regretting a decision he took this morning." hears the value the structure most often carries, but a regret looks back at a choice that was made, and the dispatcher names no choice at all, only a timetable. And "He is ordering the driver to telephone him before four o'clock." turns a remark made to a colleague, about a van that is far away, into an instruction that nobody in the van can hear.

questions.prompt: A youth centre in Gafsa pins up this notice. "ASSISTANT LIBRARIAN, six months, part-time. The work: shelving, lending, and helping pupils find what they need. Who may apply: candidates who hold a two-year degree in documentation AND have done at least one internship in a library. Training: two weeks, paid, before you start. Applications close on 30 April." Four young people from the town read it on the same afternoon. Which one may apply?

options.text: Hichem, who has a two-year degree in documentation and has never set foot in a library except as a reader.
Sonia, who has done two internships in a library and left university after her first year.
Rania, who has a two-year degree in documentation and did a month's internship in a library last year.
Mehdi, who has a two-year degree in documentation, one internship, and posted his letter on 2 May.

questions.explanation: "Rania, who has a two-year degree in documentation and did a month's internship in a library last year." is the only one who may apply: the notice joins its two conditions with AND, so both have to be met, and she is the one who holds the degree and has served the internship, in time. "Hichem, who has a two-year degree in documentation and has never set foot in a library except as a reader." meets the first condition and fails the second, and with AND one condition out of two is nothing. "Sonia, who has done two internships in a library and left university after her first year." fails the other way round: two internships do not replace the qualification the notice asks for, and one year is not the two-year degree. And "Mehdi, who has a two-year degree in documentation, one internship, and posted his letter on 2 May." meets both conditions and still cannot be considered, because the notice closes on 30 April; a date at the bottom of an advertisement is a condition like the others.
